Each hole represents a sample collected from rocks on the Martian surface; Curiosity’s drill, located on the end of its robotic arm, drops pulverized rock samples into instruments in its belly that analyze their composition. items.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
items.snippet: Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

items.snippet: A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.

items.title: James Webb telescope spots giant star swallowing its companion in first-ever observations of a stellar merger
items.snippet: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope followed up on years-old observations to confirm the first recorded act of a giant star swallowing its companion. The stellar cannibalism occurred just next door, in the Andromeda galaxy.

items.title: An Anthropic mathematician claims to have proven the Riemann hypothesis. We have to rethink how we reward expertise.
items.snippet: AI has upended the math community with a flood of results. We have to rethink how we assess which questions and answers matter — putting humans back at the center.

items.title: Ghostly 'sand body' double burial unearthed at Sutton Hoo
items.snippet: During a month-long excavation with the documentary series "Time Team," archaeologists unearthed another mysterious "sand body" at Sutton Hoo.

items.title: Quantum entanglement could thwart hackers and scammers, physicists reveal
items.snippet: In a first-of-its-kind experiment, physicists used pairs of entangled photons to verify a person's location. That's a step toward anchoring digital security to the physical world.

items.title: Two massive stars may be secretly feeding the Milky Way’s supermassive black hole
items.snippet: Astronomers have traced mysterious gas clouds near the Milky Way's central supermassive black hole to a massive pair of stars whose colliding winds appear to create dense clumps of material. These clouds may eventually feed the black hole, revealing a surprising connection between stellar activity and the growth of cosmic giants.

items.title: CERN scientists finally find evidence of a particle decay so rare it took 40 years to detect
items.snippet: Scientists at CERN have found the first evidence of an incredibly rare particle decay after more than 40 years of searching, detecting a process expected to occur just once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The breakthrough could help physicists explore a mysterious microscopic realm where unknown particles and forces may be hiding.

items.title: Scientists turn Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks for future lunar bases
items.snippet: Scientists have found a way to 3D-print Moon dust into LEGO-like bricks, raising the possibility of building lunar bases using materials already on the Moon. The experimental blocks still need to be strengthened, but the technology could transform how humans construct permanent settlements beyond Earth.

items.title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
items.snippet: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

items.title: X-ray technique advances temperature measurements under extreme pressure
items.snippet: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) have advanced the ability to measure temperatures in materials subjected to extreme pressures at the National Ignition Facility (NIF), providing new insights into how materials behave under conditions relevant to national security and high-energy-density physics.

items.title: Parasite protein expands understanding of how mitochondria build their ribosomes
items.snippet: Mitochondria are essential components of the cells of most organisms, including humans. They are often referred to as the cell's powerhouses because they produce the energy needed for cellular functions. However, mitochondria originally evolved from free-living bacteria that were engulfed by other cells in the distant past.

items.title: Mapping the microbes' arms race with viruses at planetary scale
items.snippet: Microbiomes are complex ecosystems, in which bacteria and archaea are constantly interacting with, and infected by, viruses. These viruses can significantly impact microbiome processes, not only by killing their host but also sometimes by temporarily providing additional capabilities to their host. items.title: El Niño created a skiers' paradise in Chile—now it's Sierra Nevada and southern Rockies' turn
items.snippet: El Niño has a reputation for being a skier's dream, bringing lots of snow to California's Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño's supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

items.title: Practical organ-on-a-chip platform helps assess the toxicity of environmental chemicals
items.snippet: Among the thousands of chemicals used in daily life, toxicity information is available for only a small fraction. Much of this information comes from high-dose animal studies, which are costly, time-consuming and limited by species differences.

items.title: New sources of neurotoxin linked to algal blooms uncovered in Florida and Kansas
items.snippet: Researchers have identified two previously unreported strains of freshwater cyanobacteria capable of producing a potent neurotoxin that poses risks to people, pets, wildlife and water resources and that some scientists suspect may have contributed to previous animal deaths.

items.title: Bumblebees challenge long-held beliefs about brain size and intelligence
items.snippet: Bigger brains mean greater intelligence, or so conventional wisdom goes. After all, humans have much larger brains than most other animals and are generally considered the planet's most intelligent species.

items.title: Is it genuine love—or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts

items.title: Clean energy choices shape environmental impacts beyond greenhouse gas emissions
items.snippet: The burning of fossil fuels such as coal, gas and oil is the primary driver of climate change, but clean energy strategies to achieve net-zero greenhouse gas emissions do not systematically alleviate other environmental problems. In fact, some pathways add pressure on natural resources like land, water and minerals.
